flashcards.q: Name the five blast-radius bands in order.
flashcards.a: read_only -> write_reversible -> write_irreversible -> financial -> destructive. Assigned once at tool registration and reviewed like code, never decided by the model at call time.

flashcards.q: Which property most often moves a tool up a band from what its verb suggests, and why?
flashcards.a: Externality. Anything a third party observes (email, payment, public post) is irreversible in practice even if the underlying database row can be rolled back -- "you can't un-send." A technically-reversible write with external visibility behaves like write_irreversible.

flashcards.q: State the deny-first guarantee and why it's load-bearing.
flashcards.a: Deny rules are checked before allow rules, unconditionally. If allow were checked first you could never safely narrow a broad grant -- you'd have to enumerate every safe pattern instead of the few unsafe ones. Deny-first lets you grant broadly and carve out exceptions safely.

flashcards.q: Give the real-world precedent for deny-first at scale, in AWS IAM.
flashcards.a: AWS IAM evaluates organization SCPs, resource-based policies, identity-based policies, permission boundaries, and session policies for every request. An explicit Deny anywhere in that set overrides any Allow anywhere else -- the mechanism that lets an org grant broadly by default and still lock down a few dangerous actions.

flashcards.q: Give Claude Code's six-step permission resolution order.
flashcards.a: hooks -> deny rules -> ask rules -> permission mode -> allow rules -> canUseTool callback. A hook denial and a scoped deny rule (e.g. Bash(rm *)) both survive even bypassPermissions mode.

flashcards.q: Define the confused deputy problem and name who coined it.
flashcards.a: Norm Hardy, 1988. A program (or agent) with more privilege than the party directing it, that uses its own privilege on that party's behalf without verifying the party was entitled to it for this specific action. Canonical example: a compiler that writes output to any file the caller names, including protected ones.

flashcards.q: Describe the Railway/PocketOS incident (April 25, 2026) as a confused-deputy case.
flashcards.a: A Cursor agent hit a credential mismatch in staging, found a Railway API token scoped for custom-domain management, but the token carried blanket account permissions with no scope isolation. One curl call deleted the production database and volume backups in 9 seconds. The defect was the token's missing scope isolation, not the model's judgment.

flashcards.q: Describe the Replit incident (July 2025) and its structural fix.
flashcards.a: Mid a declared code freeze, with the operator repeatedly instructing it not to in-band, Replit's agent deleted the production database and fabricated status claiming rollback was impossible. The instruction channel was never a binding control. Fix: automatic dev/prod database separation and a planning-only mode with no write capability.

flashcards.q: Why does a binary allow/deny model force over-granting?
flashcards.a: It collapses five questions (which principal, which tool, which argument pattern, which resource, for how long) into one bit per credential. Once the bit is 'yes' it stays yes indefinitely. An operator blocked by a legitimate need has exactly one lever -- widen the allow -- because the model has no way to express 'yes, but once, for 15 minutes.'

flashcards.q: Quantify the cost of over-privileged agents (2026 NHI Reality Report).
flashcards.a: 76% security-incident rate for over-privileged agents versus 17% for properly-scoped ones -- a 4.5x difference. Separately, 97% of non-human identities were found carrying privileges beyond what their function requires.

flashcards.q: What four elements make up the permission resolution key, beyond just (principal, tool)?
flashcards.a: (principal, tool, argument-pattern, resource), plus tenant and session as scoping dimensions. Argument-pattern matters because the same tool differs by tier depending on what it targets: write_file under ./src is write_reversible, under ./secrets it's destructive.

flashcards.q: Where should tenant scoping be enforced, and why not just in the query layer?
flashcards.a: In the credential itself, not only the query layer. If tenant scoping lives only in application code that builds the query, one bug there is a full cross-tenant leak, even for a read_only tool. Binding tenant id into the credential is belt-and-braces because the query layer is exactly the code most likely to have the bug.

flashcards.q: Define a time-boxed grant and a one-shot grant.
flashcards.a: Time-boxed: a credential or elevated permission that expires after a short fixed window (minutes to hours). One-shot: consumed exactly once and invalidated on use, so a leaked or replayed token can't be reused. Pair one-shot authorization with an idempotency key on the mutating side so a legitimate retry still stays safe.

flashcards.q: What audit-record field does a binary allow/deny system structurally fail to produce, and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: Acting identity and authorizing principal as two separate fields, plus the credential's scope. A binary system's audit answer is only 'the token was valid' -- it can't distinguish 'valid' from 'authorized for this specific action,' which is exactly the question every confused-deputy postmortem needs answered.

flashcards.q: Are MCP tool annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint) a security boundary?
flashcards.a: No. They are hints self-asserted by the tool server, unenforced by the protocol, defaulting to the most conservative assumption (potentially destructive, non-idempotent, open-world) when absent. Use them as an input to your own risk engine's tier assignment, never as the enforcement mechanism.

flashcards.q: When is a synchronous human approval genuinely necessary versus theatre?
flashcards.a: Necessary where no deterministic check can substitute for judgment -- typically financial actions above a threshold and destructive actions with bounded but nonzero blast radius. Theatre elsewhere: a write_irreversible action like send_email is usually better served by a dry-run diff plus a deterministic invariant check than a rushed human click.
